title: Young and dyslexic? You've got it going on
author: Benjamin Zephaniah
blurb: An article about overcoming prejudice at school and seeing dyslexia as a creative advantage, built on personal anecdote and humour.
source: Published in The Guardian, Friday 2 October 2015
heading: Young and dyslexic? You've got it going on - Benjamin Zephaniah
context: As a child I suffered, but learned to turn dyslexia to my advantage, to see the world more creatively. We are the architects, we are the designers.

paragraphs.html: I'm of the generation where teachers didn't know what dyslexia was. The big problem with the education system then was that there was no compassion, no understanding and no humanity. I don't look back and feel angry with the teachers. The ones who wanted to have an individual approach weren't allowed to. The idea of being kind and thoughtful and listening to problems just wasn't done: the past is a different kind of country.

At school my ideas always contradicted the teachers'. I remember one teacher saying that human beings sleep for one-third of their life and I put my hand up and said, "If there's a God isn't that a design fault? If you've built something, you want efficiency. If I was God I would have designed sleep so we could stay awake. Then good people could do one-third more good in the world."

The teacher said, "Shut up, stupid boy. Bad people would do one-third more bad." I thought I'd put in a good idea. I was just being creative. She also had a point, but the thing was, she called me stupid for even thinking about it.

I remember a teacher talking about Africa and the 'local savages' and I would say, "Who are you to talk about savages?" She would say, "How dare you challenge me?" – and that would get me into trouble.

Once, when I was finding it difficult to engage with writing and had asked for some help, a teacher said, "It's all right. We can't all be intelligent, but you'll end up being a good sportsperson, so why don't you go outside and play some football?" I thought, "Oh great", but now I realise he was stereotyping me.

I had poems in my head even then, and when I was 10 or 11 my sister wrote some of them down for me. When I was 13 I could read very basically but it would be such hard work that I would give up. I thought that so long as you could read how much the banknote was worth, you knew enough or you could ask a mate.

I got thrown out of a lot of schools, the last one at 13. I was expelled partly because of arguing with teachers on an intellectual level and partly for being a rude boy and fighting. I didn't stab anybody, but I did take revenge on a teacher once. I stole his car and drove it into his front garden. I remember him telling us the Nazis weren't that bad. He could say that in the classroom. When I was in borstal I used to do this thing of looking at people I didn't want to be like. I saw a guy who spent all his time sitting stooped over and I thought, "I don't want to be like that," so I learned to sit with a straight back. Being observant helped me make the right choices.

A high percentage of the prison population are dyslexic, and a high percentage of the architect population. If you look at the statistics, I should be in prison: a black man brought up on the wrong side of town whose family fell apart, in trouble with the police when I was a kid, unable to read and write, with no qualifications and, on top of that, dyslexic. But I think staying out of prison is about conquering your fears and finding your path in life.

When I go into prisons to talk to people I see men and women who, in intelligence and other qualities, are the same as me. But opportunities opened for me and they missed theirs, didn't notice them or didn't take them.

I never thought I was stupid. I didn't have that struggle. If I have someone in front of me who doesn't have a problem reading and writing telling me that black people are savages I just think, "I'm not stupid – you're the one who's stupid." I just had self-belief.

For my first book I told my poems to my girlfriend, who wrote them down for me. It really took off, especially within the black community. I wrote 'wid luv' for 'with love'. People didn't think they were dyslexic poems, they just thought I wrote phonetically.

At 21 I went to an adult education class in London to learn to read and write. The teacher told me, "You are dyslexic," and I was like, "Do I need an operation?" She explained to me what it meant and I suddenly thought, "Ah, I get it. I thought I was going crazy."

I wrote more poetry, novels for teenagers, plays, other books and recorded music. I take poetry to people who do not read poetry. Still now, when I'm writing the word 'knot', I have to stop and think, "How do I write that?" I have to draw something to let me know what the word is to come back to it later. If I can't spell 'question' I just put a question mark and come back to it later.

When I look at a book, the first thing I see is the size of it, and I know that's what it's like for a lot of young people who find reading tough. When Brunel University offered me the job of professor of poetry and creative writing, I knew my students would be officially more educated than me. I tell them, "You can do this course and get the right grade because you have a good memory – but if you don't have passion, creativity, individuality, there's no point." In my life now, I find that people accommodate my dyslexia. I can perform my poetry because it doesn't have to be word perfect, but I never read one of my novels in public. When I go to literary festivals I always get an actor to read it out for me. Otherwise all my energy goes into reading the book and the mood is lost.

If someone can't understand dyslexia it's their problem. In the same way, if someone oppresses me because of my race I don't sit down and think, "How can I become white?" It's not my problem, it's theirs and they are the ones who have to come to terms with it. If you're dyslexic and you feel there's something holding you back, just remember: it's not you. In many ways being dyslexic is a natural way to be.

What's unnatural is the way we read and write. If you look at a pictorial language like Chinese, you can see the word for a woman because the character looks like a woman. The word for a house looks like a house. It is a strange step to go from that to a squiggle that represents a sound.

So don't be heavy on yourself. And if you are a parent of someone with dyslexia don't think of it as a defect. Dyslexia is not a measure of intelligence: you may have a genius on your hands. Having dyslexia can make you creative. If you want to construct a sentence and can't find the word you are searching for, you have to think of a way to write round it. This requires being creative and so your 'creativity muscle' gets bigger.

Kids come up to me and say, "I'm dyslexic too," and I say to them, "Use it to your advantage, see the world differently. Us dyslexic people, we've got it going on – we are the architects. We are the designers." It's like these kids are proud to be like me and if that helps them, that is great. I didn't have that as a child. I say to them, "Bloody non-dyslexics ... who do they think they are?"

generation-teachers.quote: I'm of the generation where teachers didn't know what dyslexia was
generation-teachers.what: Establishes historical context - dyslexia wasn't recognised or understood.
generation-teachers.effect: Shows this isn't personal failure but systemic ignorance. Sets up critique of education.

big-problem.quote: The big problem with the education system then was that there was no compassion, no understanding and no humanity
big-problem.what: Triple negative 'no compassion, no understanding, no humanity' emphasises complete failure.
big-problem.effect: Damning indictment of education system. Shows emotional damage beyond academic struggle.

dont-look-back.quote: I don't look back and feel angry with the teachers
dont-look-back.what: Shows emotional maturity and ability to forgive despite suffering.
dont-look-back.effect: Unexpected forgiveness disarms readers. Shows he's moved beyond bitterness.

ones-who-wanted.quote: The ones who wanted to have an individual approach weren't allowed to
ones-who-wanted.what: Distinguishes between individual teachers and oppressive system.
ones-who-wanted.effect: Shows problem was structural not personal - some teachers wanted to help but couldn't.

past-different.quote: The idea of being kind and thoughtful and listening to problems just wasn't done: the past is a different kind of country
past-different.what: References L.P. Hartley's 'The past is a foreign country' - literary sophistication.
past-different.effect: Shows his education despite dyslexia. Creates temporal distance from trauma.

ideas-contradicted.quote: At school my ideas always contradicted the teachers'
ideas-contradicted.what: 'Always' shows consistent pattern of challenging authority.
ideas-contradicted.effect: Sets up pattern of creative thinking being suppressed. He thought differently from the start.

remember-teacher.quote: I remember one teacher saying that human beings sleep for one-third of their life and I put my hand up and said, 'If there's a God isn't that a design fault?'
remember-teacher.what: Shows child Zephaniah asking profound philosophical questions.
remember-teacher.effect: Demonstrates intelligence and creativity despite being labelled stupid. Questions everything.

shut-up-stupid.quote: The teacher said, 'Shut up, stupid boy. Bad people would do one-third more bad.'
shut-up-stupid.what: Harsh direct quote shows brutal dismissal of creative thinking.
shut-up-stupid.effect: Shocking cruelty of response. Reader feels the child's humiliation.

thought-good-idea.quote: I thought I'd put in a good idea. I was just being creative. She also had a point, but the thing was, she called me stupid for even thinking about it
thought-good-idea.what: Shows he could see teacher's point but objects to being called stupid for thinking.
thought-good-idea.effect: Reasonable tone makes teacher's cruelty worse. Thinking itself was punished.

teacher-africa.quote: I remember a teacher talking about Africa and the 'local savages' and I would say, 'Who are you to talk about savages?'
teacher-africa.what: Young Zephaniah challenges racist colonial attitudes directly.
teacher-africa.effect: Shows moral intelligence - recognised racism when supposedly educated adults didn't.

how-dare.quote: She would say, 'How dare you challenge me?'
how-dare.what: Teacher's response about authority not accuracy - power threatened.
how-dare.effect: Shows education was about obedience not truth. Questions weren't welcome.

difficult-engage.quote: Once, when I was finding it difficult to engage with writing and had asked for some help, a teacher said, 'It's all right. We can't all be intelligent, but you'll end up being a good sportsperson'
difficult-engage.what: Teacher's response combines low expectations with racial stereotyping.
difficult-engage.effect: Shows intersection of dyslexia and racism. Double discrimination.

oh-great.quote: I thought, 'Oh great', but now I realise he was stereotyping me
oh-great.what: Child's innocent response versus adult understanding of racism.
oh-great.effect: Shows how children internalise discrimination before understanding it.

poems-head.quote: I had poems in my head even then, and when I was 10 or 11 my sister wrote some of them down for me
poems-head.what: Proves creative ability existed despite inability to write.
poems-head.effect: Creativity preceded literacy - natural poet trapped by dyslexia.

thirteen-read.quote: When I was 13 I could read very basically but it would be such hard work that I would give up
thirteen-read.what: Reading possible but exhausting - explains why he gave up.
thirteen-read.effect: Makes dyslexia concrete - not inability but exhaustion.

banknote-worth.quote: I thought that so long as you could read how much the banknote was worth, you knew enough or you could ask a mate
banknote-worth.what: Child's practical approach to literacy - just enough to survive.
banknote-worth.effect: Shows resourcefulness and adaptation. Makes do with minimal literacy.

thrown-out.quote: I got thrown out of a lot of schools, the last one at 13
thrown-out.what: Matter-of-fact about multiple expulsions - normalised failure.
thrown-out.effect: Shows system repeatedly failed him. Pattern of rejection.

expelled-partly.quote: I was expelled partly because of arguing with teachers on an intellectual level and partly for being a rude boy and fighting
expelled-partly.what: Honest about both intellectual and physical rebellion.
expelled-partly.effect: Not romanticising - admits violence alongside intellectual challenge.

didnt-stab.quote: I didn't stab anybody, but I did take revenge on a teacher once. I stole his car and drove it into his front garden
didnt-stab.what: 'Didn't stab anybody' as baseline shows how bad things got.
didnt-stab.effect: Shocking honesty. Shows depth of anger and alienation.

nazis-not-bad.quote: I remember him telling us the Nazis weren't that bad
nazis-not-bad.what: Explains extreme response - teacher was Nazi sympathiser.
nazis-not-bad.effect: Suddenly car theft seems more justified. Teachers weren't moral authorities.

borstal-observant.quote: When I was in borstal I used to do this thing of looking at people I didn't want to be like
borstal-observant.what: Even in borstal, actively learning and making choices.
borstal-observant.effect: Shows determination to grow even in worst circumstances.

high-percentage.quote: A high percentage of the prison population are dyslexic, and a high percentage of the architect population
high-percentage.what: Juxtaposes prison and architecture - same condition, different outcomes.
high-percentage.effect: Shows dyslexia leads to extremes - creativity or criminalisation.

look-statistics.quote: If you look at the statistics, I should be in prison: a black man brought up on the wrong side of town whose family fell apart
look-statistics.what: Lists every statistical predictor of imprisonment.
look-statistics.effect: Makes his success more remarkable. Should have failed by every measure.

staying-out.quote: But I think staying out of prison is about conquering your fears and finding your path in life
staying-out.effect: Offers hope through personal responsibility and self-discovery.

go-prisons.quote: When I go into prisons to talk to people I see men and women who, in intelligence and other qualities, are the same as me
go-prisons.what: Acknowledges prisoners as equals, not inferiors.
go-prisons.effect: Shows humility and solidarity. Luck not superiority saved him.

opportunities-opened.quote: But opportunities opened for me and they missed theirs, didn't notice them or didn't take them
opportunities-opened.what: Life paths diverged through opportunities not inherent difference.
opportunities-opened.effect: Makes success feel precarious - could easily have gone wrong.

never-thought-stupid.quote: I never thought I was stupid. I didn't have that struggle
never-thought-stupid.what: Core self-belief remained despite constant messaging.
never-thought-stupid.effect: Shows remarkable psychological resilience. Internal strength crucial.

black-savages.quote: If I have someone in front of me who doesn't have a problem reading and writing telling me that black people are savages I just think, 'I'm not stupid – you're the one who's stupid.'
black-savages.what: Uses teacher's racism to prove their stupidity not his.
black-savages.effect: Brilliant reversal - literacy doesn't equal intelligence or morality.

self-belief.effect: Makes self-belief seem achievable - presented simply not dramatically.

first-book.quote: For my first book I told my poems to my girlfriend, who wrote them down for me
first-book.what: Found workaround for dyslexia through collaboration.
first-book.effect: Shows creativity finds a way. Dyslexia didn't stop him publishing.

took-off.quote: It really took off, especially within the black community
took-off.what: Black community understood and valued his voice.
took-off.effect: Found his audience despite educational rejection.

wid-luv.what: Phonetic spelling became stylistic choice not error.
wid-luv.effect: Turned dyslexic spelling into authentic poetic voice.

phonetically.quote: People didn't think they were dyslexic poems, they just thought I wrote phonetically
phonetically.what: Audience assumed artistic choice not learning difficulty.
phonetically.effect: Shows how dyslexia can be invisible when reframed as style.

twenty-one.quote: At 21 I went to an adult education class in London to learn to read and write
twenty-one.what: Decisive action to address literacy as adult.
twenty-one.effect: Shows it's never too late to learn. Courage to return to education.

teacher-dyslexic.quote: The teacher told me, 'You are dyslexic,' and I was like, 'Do I need an operation?'
teacher-dyslexic.what: Humour in ignorance about dyslexia - thought it was medical.
teacher-dyslexic.effect: Makes moment of diagnosis relatable and human.

explained-meant.quote: She explained to me what it meant and I suddenly thought, 'Ah, I get it. I thought I was going crazy.'
explained-meant.what: Diagnosis brought relief - explanation not madness.
explained-meant.effect: Shows importance of diagnosis. Understanding transforms experience.

wrote-more.quote: I wrote more poetry, novels for teenagers, plays, other books and recorded music
wrote-more.effect: Proves dyslexia didn't limit creative output. Massive success.

take-poetry.quote: I take poetry to people who do not read poetry
take-poetry.what: Makes poetry accessible to non-traditional audiences.
take-poetry.effect: Uses experience to break down barriers for others.

writing-knot.quote: Still now, when I'm writing the word 'knot', I have to stop and think, 'How do I write that?' I have to draw something to let me know what the word is
writing-knot.what: Concrete example of daily dyslexic challenge with homophone.
writing-knot.effect: Shows dyslexia doesn't disappear with success. Daily reality.

cant-spell.quote: If I can't spell 'question' I just put a question mark and come back to it later
cant-spell.what: Creative workaround using symbol for word.
cant-spell.effect: Shows ongoing adaptations. Pragmatic not defeated.

look-book.quote: When I look at a book, the first thing I see is the size of it, and I know that's what it's like for a lot of young people who find reading tough
look-book.what: Still sees books as dyslexic person - remembers the struggle.
look-book.effect: Creates connection with struggling readers. Hasn't forgotten.

brunel-university.quote: When Brunel University offered me the job of professor of poetry and creative writing, I knew my students would be officially more educated than me
brunel-university.what: Expelled child becomes professor - ultimate reversal.
brunel-university.effect: Perfect irony. System that rejected him now employs him.

tell-students.quote: I tell them, 'You can do this course and get the right grade because you have a good memory – but if you don't have passion, creativity, individuality, there's no point.'
tell-students.what: Values creativity over conventional academic success.
tell-students.effect: Challenges academic values. Memory less important than creativity.

people-accommodate.quote: In my life now, I find that people accommodate my dyslexia
people-accommodate.what: Success means others adapt to him, not vice versa.
people-accommodate.effect: Power shift - world adapts to him now he's successful.

perform-poetry.quote: I can perform my poetry because it doesn't have to be word perfect, but I never read one of my novels in public
perform-poetry.what: Honest about limitations - performs poetry, doesn't read prose.
perform-poetry.effect: Shows wisdom in working with dyslexia not against it.

cant-understand.quote: If someone can't understand dyslexia it's their problem
cant-understand.what: Completely reverses usual dynamic - their ignorance, their problem.
cant-understand.effect: Powerful reframing. Refuses to carry shame.

oppresses-race.quote: In the same way, if someone oppresses me because of my race I don't sit down and think, 'How can I become white?'
oppresses-race.what: Links dyslexia discrimination to racism - both require oppressor to change.
oppresses-race.effect: Makes absurdity of expecting dyslexics to be 'normal' clear.

not-my-problem.quote: It's not my problem, it's theirs and they are the ones who have to come to terms with it
not-my-problem.what: Places responsibility on discriminator not victim.
not-my-problem.effect: Liberating message - stop trying to fix yourself.

feel-holding.quote: If you're dyslexic and you feel there's something holding you back, just remember: it's not you
feel-holding.what: Speaks directly to dyslexic readers feeling limited.
feel-holding.effect: Personal, direct comfort. You're not the problem.

natural-way.quote: In many ways being dyslexic is a natural way to be
natural-way.what: Challenges assumption that non-dyslexic is natural.
natural-way.effect: Profound reframing - maybe dyslexia is natural.

whats-unnatural.quote: What's unnatural is the way we read and write
whats-unnatural.what: Flips script - writing system is unnatural, not dyslexia.

pictorial-chinese.quote: If you look at a pictorial language like Chinese, you can see the word for a woman because the character looks like a woman
pictorial-chinese.what: Shows other writing systems more intuitive than alphabet.
pictorial-chinese.effect: Proves alphabetic writing isn't only or best system.

strange-step.quote: It is a strange step to go from that to a squiggle that represents a sound
strange-step.effect: Makes readers question assumed naturalness of alphabet.

dont-heavy.quote: So don't be heavy on yourself

parent-dyslexia.quote: And if you are a parent of someone with dyslexia don't think of it as a defect
parent-dyslexia.effect: Challenges medical/deficit model parents might adopt.

not-measure.quote: Dyslexia is not a measure of intelligence: you may have a genius on your hands
not-measure.what: Separates dyslexia from intelligence - might have genius child.
not-measure.effect: Transforms parental anxiety into excitement about potential.

make-creative.quote: Having dyslexia can make you creative. If you want to construct a sentence and can't find the word you are searching for, you have to think of a way to write round it. This requires being creative and so your 'creativity muscle' gets bigger
make-creative.what: 'Creativity muscle' makes abstract concept physical and trainable.
make-creative.effect: Shows dyslexia forces creative problem-solving. Strength through struggle.

kids-come.quote: Kids come up to me and say, 'I'm dyslexic too,'
kids-come.what: Shows his impact on young dyslexics who identify with him.
kids-come.effect: Establishes him as inspiration and role model.

use-advantage.quote: and I say to them, 'Use it to your advantage, see the world differently. Us dyslexic people, we've got it going on – we are the architects. We are the designers.'
use-advantage.what: Transforms dyslexia into superpower. 'We've got it going on' - pride and swagger.
use-advantage.effect: Creates positive dyslexic identity. Membership in creative elite.

kids-proud.quote: It's like these kids are proud to be like me and if that helps them, that is great
kids-proud.what: Acknowledges his role in transforming shame to pride.
kids-proud.effect: Shows purpose of article - helping kids feel proud not ashamed.

didnt-have.quote: I didn't have that as a child
didnt-have.what: Poignant reminder he lacked what he now provides.
didnt-have.effect: Makes his role more important - filling gap he experienced.

bloody-non.quote: I say to them, 'Bloody non-dyslexics ... who do they think they are?'
bloody-non.what: Flips discrimination with mock outrage at 'normal' people.
bloody-non.effect: Ends with humour and defiance. Makes dyslexics the in-group.

borstal.meaning: A type of youth detention centre
borstal.note: British institution for young offenders, abolished in 1982. Shows how serious his troubles became.
borstal.effect: Historical term showing the severity of his teenage rebellion and the system's punitive response.

overview.heading: Why Zephaniah Wrote This
overview.intro: Zephaniah's purposes evolve through the article:

points.label: To expose educational failings
points.text: "Teachers didn't know what dyslexia was" - Shows systemic ignorance

points.label: To reframe dyslexia positively
points.text: "Dyslexia is not a measure of intelligence" - Challenges misconceptions

points.label: To inspire young dyslexics
points.text: "We are the architects. We are the designers" - Empowers through identity

points.label: Young dyslexics
points.text: "Kids come up to me and say, 'I'm dyslexic too'" - Direct encouragement

points.label: Parents of dyslexic children
points.text: "If you are a parent of someone with dyslexia don't think of it as a defect" - Guidance

points.label: General readers
points.text: "I know that's what it's like for a lot of young people" - Creates understanding

points.label: Rebellious teenager
points.text: "I didn't stab anybody, but I did take revenge" - Defiant honesty

points.label: Reflective adult
points.text: "I don't look back and feel angry" - Mature perspective

points.label: Confident professional
points.text: "I tell them, 'You can do this course...'" - Authoritative teacher

points.label: Playful provocateur
points.text: "Bloody non-dyslexics ... who do they think they are?" - Humorous reversal

points.label: Direct quotation
points.text: "Shut up, stupid boy" - Raw, unfiltered teacher cruelty

points.label: Metaphor
points.text: "creativity muscle gets bigger" - Physical metaphor for mental development

points.label: Colloquialism
points.text: "wid luv", "we've got it going on" - Authentic voice

points.label: Irony
points.text: "the past is a different kind of country" - Borrowed literary reference

points.label: Chronological journey
points.text: From school struggles to professorship - life progression

points.label: Pivotal discovery
points.text: "At 21 I went to an adult education class" - Turning point

points.label: Cyclical return
points.text: Opens with "We are the architects" and closes with same message
